newsitem.title: UK: Physical lead market sluggish in Europe.
newsitem.headline: Physical lead market sluggish in Europe.

text.p: The European physical lead market is in the doldrums, with southern Europe especially hard-hit, traders and industry sources said.
"The physical market in Europe is depressing," one trader said.
Producers have felt the pressure and many were forced to accept softer premiums on 1997 long-term contracts after big rises last year sparked by fears of tightness.

"A lot of customers built up stocks in 1996 expecting a worse squeeze than there's been. We think a lot of our customers have been running down stocks a little bit over the past month," an industry source said.

Typical producer premiums for 99.99 percent purity material ex-works ranged from $90 to $110 over LME cash prices for recently concluded long-term contracts. In southern Europe, some premiums were down $20 from last year, traders said.
But at least one producer said it achieved a small rise in premiums this year on long-term contracts.
Spot premiums currently were largely weaker than what was achieved on the long-term contracts, although there were again regional differences between northern and southern Europe, the sources said.

Some in the market were hit by a big contract between battery manufacturer Exide and trader Glencore for 80,000 tonnes of lead, leaving some of Exide's former suppliers with excess material, they added.
But some traders and industry sources wondered where Glencore would source the material.
"Some of it will come from Kazakhstan, Bulgaria and Morocco, where they have a tolling agreement. But in my calculation they still need 30,000 tonnes," one trader said.

If secondary lead can be supplied, it may come from Quexco, which controls Europe's biggest lead recycling business. Last year it acquired the lead business of Metallgesellschaft of Germany and the lead recycling facilities of Enirisorse of Italy.
"The question is whether Glencore is going to force Metaleurop to give them the tonnage," a trader said.
Glencore International holds a 15 percent shareholding in French based metals group Metaleurop.
In the financial year ended September 30, 1996, Metaleurop's lead output fell by 50,000 tonnes to 310,000 tonnes, mostly due to difficulties experienced at its new plant in Nordenham, Germany.
Traders said the volume of warrant activity was slow on the back of the lacklustre spot market, but some premiums were holding good levels.
One said that he had done a deal for 99.985 percent eastern European material in Rotterdam for $25 over LME cash, but added other business had been done for less than that.

Other dealers said Rotterdam premiums had been going for anything between $8 and $15, which compares to $5/$10 last September. Rotterdam LME stocks have fallen to 2,075 tonnes from 5,700 tonnes at end November 1996.
Premiums in Antwerp were said to be around $25 and Genoa at $15/$20.
Total LME inventories are down to 110,900 tonnes from 122,900 in December.
On the demand side, Italy has been a particularly soft spot as the auto and ceramics sectors experience low levels of business, sources said.
In the U.S., shipments of replacement lead-acid auto batteries were down 11.09 percent in December 1996 from the previous year. For the year, shipments were little changed, up 0.21 percent from 1995.
